patients.summary: Healthy elementary school teacher with mild intermittent asthma on albuterol as needed who joins the practice in 2023 and has three term deliveries at an outside hospital between 2024 and 2026: two vaginal deliveries after labors labeled active phase arrest, then a cesarean for arrest of descent. Primary care is preventive visits, postpartum check-ins and albuterol refills.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
27 y/o woman establishing care. Moved to the hill towns last year, teaches second grade. No current concerns, mostly wants a doctor in place and her inhaler renewed.

Asthma: diagnosed as a kid. Uses albuterol maybe a few times a year. Never intubated, never hospitalized, no steroid bursts she can remember as an adult. No nighttime cough or waking. Has never been on a daily controller.

PMH: asthma, mild intermittent. No surgeries. Never pregnant.
Meds: albuterol HFA 2 puffs q4-6h prn wheeze.
Allergies: NKDA.
FH: mother with asthma, also had a C-section with her ('labor didn't progress'). Father seasonal allergies.
SH: married. Elementary school teacher. Never smoked, no vaping. Doesn't drink. Walks most evenings.
Gyn: regular cycles. Last Pap last year at her old office, she thinks it was fine. Records requested.

ROS negative except as above.

Exam: well-appearing, pleasant. HEENT normal, TMs clear. Neck supple, no adenopathy, thyroid normal size. Lungs clear throughout, good air movement, no wheeze on forced expiration. Heart regular, no murmur. Abdomen soft, nontender. Extremities warm, no edema. Skin without rash. Mood and affect normal.

PHQ-2 0.

A/P
1. Mild intermittent asthma - well controlled on rescue inhaler alone, rarely used. Albuterol refilled. Discussed that needing it more than twice a week would mean a call to us.
2. Health maintenance - baseline CBC, CMP, lipids. One-time HIV and hep C screening, she agreed. Pap due 2025 if last year's was normal, will confirm on records. Flu shot when the fall supply comes in.

Return in one year for physical.

documents.title: Lab Results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Samantha, everything from Thursday's draw looks good. Blood counts, kidney and liver tests and sugar are normal. Your LDL cholesterol is a little over the lab's flag line, which isn't a concern at your age with no other risk factors. The HIV and hepatitis C screens are negative, so those don't need repeating. Nothing to change. Enjoy the start of the school year.

documents.title: Positive pregnancy test
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Good morning! I took a home test this weekend and it was positive (twice, I didn't believe the first one). My last period started September 19. We weren't exactly planning on it this fall but we're really happy. What do I do next? Do I see you or do I need an OB? Also is my inhaler ok to keep using?

documents.title: RE: Positive pregnancy test
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Congratulations, that is wonderful news. By your dates you're about 6 weeks along. Prenatal care is best done with an obstetrics group, and I've put in a referral to the OB practice we work with most; their office will call you to set up the first visit, usually around 8-10 weeks. Yes, keep using albuterol whenever you need it - it's considered safe in pregnancy, and keeping asthma under control matters more than avoiding the inhaler. Call us anytime if something comes up in the meantime. I'll still be your doctor for everything else.

documents.title: Obstetric Discharge Summary
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL - LABOR AND DELIVERY
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 2024-06-19, discharged 2024-06-21

Patient: 28 y/o G1P0 at 39w1d (EDD 2024-06-25)

Admission diagnosis: term pregnancy in labor.
Discharge diagnoses: term intrauterine pregnancy, delivered; arrest of dilation in the active phase, corrected with oxytocin augmentation; spontaneous vaginal delivery.

Prenatal course: uncomplicated. Prenatal labs unremarkable. Mild intermittent asthma on albuterol as needed, no exacerbations in pregnancy.

Hospital course: Presented in the early morning with contractions every 3-4 minutes. Cervical change was slow over the first several hours and an epidural was placed at her request. Oxytocin augmentation was begun for the slow progress. Fetal tracing on admission was category I. About two hours into oxytocin, nursing noted 6 contractions in 10 minutes; the cervix at that check was 5 cm with intact membranes, and the tracing showed recurrent late decelerations on a baseline of 140 bpm with moderate variability and no accelerations. Oxytocin was turned off, she was repositioned to her left side and given an IV fluid bolus; contraction frequency settled and the decelerations resolved. Oxytocin was restarted at a lower rate, followed by artificial rupture of membranes with clear fluid. She then progressed steadily to complete dilation and had a spontaneous vaginal delivery of a liveborn infant. Estimated blood loss within normal limits. Maternal vital signs stable throughout labor; no fever, no maternal tachycardia.

Postpartum course uncomplicated. Ambulating, voiding, pain controlled with over-the-counter analgesics, tolerating diet.

Allergies: NKDA.
Discharge medications: albuterol HFA as needed, as before.
Follow-up: obstetrics postpartum visit in 6 weeks. Primary care as needed.

- Obstetrics attending, Labor and Delivery

documents.title: Postpartum Check-in
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Called pt after discharge summary filed. Three weeks out, says she's tired but doing well, healing fine, has her OB postpartum visit at the end of the month. No fever, no heavy bleeding, no calf pain, mood good, has help at home. Hasn't needed her inhaler. Due for annual in August - booked 8/22 9:30.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Annual. 28F, about 9 weeks after vaginal delivery of her first baby (6/19, outside hospital; labor needed oxytocin for slow progress, brief tracing concerns that resolved, uncomplicated otherwise per summary). Saw OB for the postpartum visit last month, cleared. Baby with her today, sleeping in the car seat.

She feels well. Sleep is broken, expected. Mood good - PHQ-9 3, the points are all sleep and energy. No intrusive thoughts. Going back to the classroom after Labor Day.

Asthma: no albuterol since before the baby. No cough or wheeze.

Meds: albuterol prn. NKDA.

Exam: well, tired-appearing but bright. Weight up from last year, expected postpartum. Thyroid normal. Lungs clear. Heart regular, no murmur. Abdomen soft, nontender. No edema. Normal affect.

A/P
- Health maintenance: CBC today to make sure she isn't anemic after delivery. Pap not due until 2025. Flu shot in October, can do COVID update then too.
- Asthma mild intermittent, quiet. Albuterol on hand.
- Postpartum mood fine, reviewed what to watch for and to reach out early.

RTC 1 yr.

documents.title: Obstetric Discharge Summary
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
LABOR AND DELIVERY - REGIONAL HOSPITAL
Discharge Summary
Admission 2025-06-15 / Discharge 2025-06-17

29 y/o G2P1001 at 39w2d (EDD 2025-06-20).

Diagnoses: intrauterine pregnancy at term, delivered. Active phase arrest (working diagnosis at 4 cm after 6 hours of oxytocin). Vaginal delivery.
History: mild intermittent asthma, albuterol as needed. Prior delivery 2024-06-19, vaginal, after oxytocin augmentation for slow active-phase progress. Prenatal care this pregnancy uncomplicated; prenatal labs unremarkable.

Course: Came in roughly a year after her first delivery, contracting every 3 minutes, cervix 4 cm on arrival. Epidural placed. Oxytocin started for augmentation. After 6 hours on oxytocin her exam was unchanged: 4 cm, 80% effaced, vertex at -2, with strong contractions coming every 2-3 minutes. An intrauterine pressure catheter showed an average of 220 Montevideo units over 10 minutes. The fetal heart rate pattern was reassuring throughout on continuous monitoring, with no decelerations. She was afebrile with stable vital signs.

Because she had not yet reached 6 cm, the team judged her still in latent labor by current criteria and continued oxytocin with amniotomy rather than proceed to cesarean. She subsequently made cervical change, reached complete dilation and delivered vaginally a liveborn infant. Uncomplicated third stage.

Postpartum: routine. Discharged home postpartum day 2 in good condition.
Allergies: NKDA.
Home meds at discharge: albuterol inhaler as needed.
Follow-up: OB office 6 weeks.

Dictated by obstetrics hospitalist.

A/P
1. Preventive - Pap today (last 2022 normal). Labs not needed this year, normal CBC last August. Flu and COVID vaccines in the fall.
2. Mild intermittent asthma - stable, no change.
3. Postpartum mood - fine. She knows to message if that changes.

See in a year.

documents.title: Obstetric Discharge Summary
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL - OBSTETRICS
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted: 2026-04-05   Discharged: 2026-04-08
Procedure: primary low transverse cesarean delivery, 2026-04-05

30 y/o G3P2002 at 38w1d by first-trimester ultrasound (EDD 2026-04-18).

Discharge diagnoses:
1. Intrauterine pregnancy at term, delivered by cesarean
2. Arrest of descent, fetal head in right occiput transverse
3. Mild intermittent asthma

Relevant history: two prior labors, 2024-06-19 and 2025-06-15, each with active phase arrest, both ending in vaginal delivery. Prenatal course this pregnancy unremarkable, prenatal labs unremarkable.

Hospital course: Admitted in active labor and progressed to complete dilation with an epidural in place. Second stage: she pushed well for 3 hours with adequate contractions. The vertex came down to +1 station early and then made no further descent over the final hour. On exam the cervix was fully dilated and effaced, the head at +1 with the sagittal suture in the right occiput transverse position. The fetal heart rate tracing was reassuring. Maternal vital signs were stable; she denied pain, only exhaustion. With arrest of descent at +1 in a transverse position, operative vaginal delivery was not an option, and after discussion she consented to cesarean. Low transverse cesarean under the existing epidural, liveborn infant, no intraoperative complications.

Postoperative course uncomplicated. Pain controlled on oral medication, tolerating diet, ambulating, incision clean and dry. Discharged postoperative day 3.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.
Discharge medications:
- Ibuprofen 600 mg PO every 6 hours as needed for incisional pain (new, short course)
- Albuterol HFA 2 puffs every 4-6 hours as needed (home medication)
Follow-up: OB incision check in 1-2 weeks, postpartum visit at 6 weeks. PCP follow-up after discharge.

- Obstetrics attending

documents.body: Spoke with pt after discharge summary arrived. Home since Wed after C-section on 4/5. Sore but managing with ibuprofen. Incision looks fine to her, no redness or drainage, no fever. Bleeding lighter each day. No leg swelling, no SOB, no wheezing. OB incision check is Friday. Scheduled PCP follow-up for early May; she'd like after the school's spring break week.

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: 30F here about 6.5 weeks after her third delivery, a cesarean on 4/5 for arrest of descent (head stuck transverse at +1 after 3 h of pushing) - her first two were vaginal. Summary reviewed. Saw OB for incision check and the 6-week visit last week; OB happy with healing. She stopped the ibuprofen about two weeks ago, no pain now except when lifting the toddler. No fevers. Bleeding has stopped. No calf pain, no SOB. Bowel and bladder normal.

Mood: honest that it's a lot with three under two, but says she's ok. PHQ-9 4, mostly sleep and energy, no anhedonia, no thoughts of self-harm. Has help.

Asthma: fine, no albuterol since the fall.

Meds: albuterol prn. NKDA.

O: Vitals reviewed, normal. Looks tired, in good spirits. Lungs clear. Heart regular. Abdomen soft, Pfannenstiel incision well healed, no erythema or tenderness. Calves soft, nontender. Normal affect.

A/P
1. Status post cesarean delivery - recovering well. CBC today. Added to surgical history.
2. Postpartum mood - screen negative. Reviewed warning signs; she has our cell.
3. Mild intermittent asthma - stable.
4. Physical due in the fall; front desk to book.
